Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
**It’s not a bug – it’s the intended behaviour of MapLibre GL JS when the style has no `glyphs` URL.**  

When `glyphs` is omitted, MapLibre falls back to **local-font rendering**. Every name you put in `text-font` is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list:

1. **If the browser can find a matching system font** → it uses that font.  
2. **If you have declared a web-font with `@font-face` (or via `map.setFontFaces()`)** → the browser loads that file and uses it.  
3. **If nothing matches** → the browser picks its generic fallback (usually “sans-serif”), which is why you see a “generic” font on the map.

So the fact that you see text at all is correct; the fact that it isn’t the exact font you named simply means the font wasn’t available locally.

---

## What’s really happening under the hood

| Step | What MapLibre does | Why it matters for you |
|------|-------------------|------------------------|
| **Style parsing** | No `glyphs` field → “local-fonts mode”. | No glyph-PBF requests are ever made. |
| **`text-font` resolution** | The array (e.g. `["My Fancy Font Bold", "sans-serif"]`) is passed to the browser’s text layout engine, exactly like a CSS `font-family` list. | The engine looks for a font with that *postscript* name on the system or in any loaded `@font-face` rules. |
| **Font loading** | If you have a matching `@font-face` rule, the browser fetches the URL you gave it. If you call `map.setFontFaces()` you can also supply a `font-faces` block from the style, which MapLibre will turn into `@font-face` rules for you. | This is where you can make your custom font appear. |
| **Fallback** | If the name cannot be resolved, the browser falls back to the next name in the list, eventually ending up at its generic default. | That is the “generic font” you’re seeing. |
| **Rendering** | The text is rendered with the browser’s native text rasterizer (SDF is not used because there are no glyph PBFs). | The result looks crisp at any zoom, but the exact shape depends on the local font file. |

> **Note:** In GL JS ≥ 5.11.0 this local-font path is *first-class* – it is not a “fallback after a failed glyph request”, it is the normal code path when `glyphs` is missing.

---

## How to get the exact font you want

### 1. Make sure the font is actually available locally

#### a. System font
* Install the font on the OS that runs the browser (or on the device for mobile browsers).  
* Use the exact **PostScript name** (the name you see in Font Book, Windows Font Viewer, or `fc-list`) in `text-font`.

#### b. Web-font via `@font-face`
```css
@font-face {
  font-family: "My Fancy Font";
  src: url("/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 400;
  font-style: normal;
}
```
* The `font-family` value **must match** the string you put in `text-font`.  
* The URL must be reachable from the page (CORS-allowed if on a different origin).  

#### c. `font-faces` property in the style (MapLibre-GL-JS ≥ 6.7.0)
If you prefer to keep everything inside the style JSON, add a `font-faces` block:

```json
{
  "font-faces": {
    "My Fancy Font": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-FFFF"]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Then, after creating the map, tell MapLibre to read it:

```js
map.on('load', () => {
  // If the style already contains the block, this is a no-op.
  // If you want to add/replace at runtime:
  map.setFontFaces(style['font-faces']);
});
```

### 2. Verify the name matches exactly

* **Case-sensitive** – `"My Fancy Font"` ≠ `"my fancy font"`.  
* **Spaces and punctuation** must be identical.  
* If you’re using a weight variant (`Bold`, `Italic`, etc.) you can either:
  * List the exact variant name in `text-font` (e.g. `["My Fancy Font Bold"]`), **or**
  * Use the generic family name and let CSS weight/italic properties apply (e.g. `["My Fancy Font"]` with `text-weight: "bold"`).

### 3. Check the browser console

* Look for **`Failed to load resource: net::ERR_ABORTED`** messages that point to your font URL.  
* Look for **`Unable to load glyph range … Rendering codepoint … locally instead.`** – this only appears when a `glyphs` URL is present and fails; it will *not* appear in pure local-font mode.

### 4. Optional: Keep a `glyphs` URL as a safety net (older GL JS)

If you need to support older MapLibre versions (< 5.11) that *require* a `glyphs` URL, you can:

```json
"glyphs": "https://myserver.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"
```

*Serve the same font stack you use locally, or just point at the public demo server (`https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`).*  
When the browser can’t find the local font, the glyph PBF will be fetched and used, so you never end up with invisible text.

---

## Common pitfalls & how to fix them

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Text appears, but in a different weight (e.g., regular instead of bold) | You listed `"My Fancy Font Bold"` but only loaded the regular TTF/WOFF. | Load the bold variant as a separate `@font-face` with `font-weight: 700` and reference it as `"My Fancy Font"` + `text-weight: "bold"` (or list the exact name). |
| No text at all (layer disappears) | Using an old MapLibre version (< 5.11) **and** no `glyphs` URL. | Upgrade MapLibre or add a `glyphs` URL. |
| Text shows, but characters from a non-Latin script are missing or look wrong | The font you loaded does not contain those Unicode ranges. | Add a `unicode-range` entry in `font-faces` that points to a font file covering those code points, or add a second font to the `text-font` fallback list (e.g., `["My Fancy Font", "Noto Sans CJK SC"]`). |
| Console shows CORS errors when loading the font file | Font URL is on a different origin without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. | Serve the font with proper CORS headers, or host it on the same origin. |
| Font loads on desktop but not on mobile | Mobile browsers sometimes block cross-origin fonts unless the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header includes the requesting origin **and** the `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` header is not set. | Ensure the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or the specific origin) **without** `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`. |

---

## TL;DR checklist

1. **Confirm you’re on MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.11** (local-fonts mode is only guaranteed from that version).  
2. **Make the font available locally** – either install it on the OS, add an `@font-face` rule, **or** use the style’s `font-faces` block + `map.setFontFaces()`.  
3. **Match the name exactly** between `text-font` and the `font-family` you declared.  
4. **Check the console** for loading errors or CORS problems.  
5. (Optional) **Add a `glyphs` URL** if you need to support older MapLibre versions or want a fallback when the local font can’t be loaded.

Once the font is reachable and the name matches, the map will render the labels in the exact typeface you specified. The generic font you’re seeing now is simply the browser’s default fallback because it couldn’t locate the requested font. It’s expected behavior, not a bug.

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR **MapLibre Native on Android can render all labels from fonts that you ship with the app – you just have to:** 1. **Bundle the TTF/OTF files in your APK (e.g. `src/main/assets/fonts/`).** 2. **Add a `font-faces` section to the style JSON that points at those files with `file:///android_asset/...` URLs.** 3. **Make sure every `text-font` name used in the style matches a key in `font-faces`.** 4. **Give the style a *dummy* `glyphs` URL (it can point at a non-existent file or a tiny empty PBF).** 5. **Load the style with `MapLibreMapOptions` / `MapView` as you normally would.** When the style is parsed, MapLibre Native will read the `font-faces` entries, load the fonts from the APK, and use HarfBuzz shaping to draw every script (Latin, Arabic, Devanagari, CJK, …). Because the glyphs URL never succeeds, the engine falls back to the local fonts – no external glyph server is required. Below is a step-by-step guide, plus a few gotchas for the most common scripts. --- ## 1. Put the font files in the APK ``` app/ └─ src/ └─ main/ └─ assets/ └─ fonts/ ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf ├─ NotoSans-Bold.ttf ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf ├─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf ← optional, huge (~30 MB) ``` *Tip:* If you only need a subset of CJK you can ship a “compact” CJK font (e.g. Noto Sans SC Compact) to keep the APK size reasonable. --- ## 2. Add a `font-faces` block to your style JSON ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/empty/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", // dummy, see §4 "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Regular": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"] // Latin, Latin-Extended } ], "Noto Sans Bold": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Bold.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"] } ], "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF"] } ], "Noto Sans Devanagari": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ], "Noto Sans CJK SC": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF", "U+20000-2A6DF"] } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Bold", "Noto Sans Regular" ], "text-size": 14 } } // … other layers … ] } ``` ### Why the `unicode-range`? * It tells the engine which characters each file actually covers. * Characters **outside** any declared range will fall back to the `glyphs` URL (which we deliberately make unavailable, so they will simply be invisible – that’s why you must list *all* scripts you intend to use). --- ## 3. Use the same `text-font` names in your layers The `text-font` array is a **fallback list**. The first name that matches a loaded font-face wins. If you want a bold weight for Latin but regular weight for Arabic, you can do: ```json "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Bold", // Latin, Greek, Cyrillic "Noto Sans Arabic", // Arabic "Noto Sans Devanagari", // Devanagari "Noto Sans CJK SC" // CJK ] ``` Because the engine reads `font-faces` first, it never contacts a glyph server for any of those scripts. --- ## 4. Provide a *dummy* `glyphs` URL MapLibre Native still expects the `glyphs` field to exist (the spec requires it). You can point it at a location that will **always fail** – the engine will then try the local `font-faces` and, if a character is not covered, simply skip drawing it. ```json "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/empty/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" ``` Create an empty file `assets/empty/` (any folder) and put a **single tiny PBF** (or nothing at all). When the engine tries to fetch `…/Noto%20Sans%20Regular/0-255.pbf` it gets a 404, logs a warning, and falls back to the local font. *If you prefer not to have a dummy file at all, you can use a non-existent scheme such as `glyphs": "null://{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"` – the request will fail instantly.* --- ## 5. Load the style in Android ```kotlin class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() { private lateinit var mapView: MapView override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) { super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) // 1️⃣ Inflate layout that contains a MapView setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView) // 2️⃣ Tell MapLibre where the style lives (inside assets) val styleUri = "file:///android_asset/style.json" // 3️⃣ Create the map with the usual options mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap -> mapboxMap.loadStyleUri(styleUri) { // style is now loaded, fonts are ready // you can also call mapboxMap.setCamera(...) etc. } } } override fun onStart() { super.onStart() mapView.onStart() } override fun onStop() { super.onStop() mapView.onStop() } // … other lifecycle callbacks … } ``` *No extra SDK calls are needed – MapLibre Native reads `font-faces` automatically (since Android 11.13.0).* --- ## 6. Special script notes | Script | What you must do | Why | |--------|------------------|-----| | **Latin / Greek / Cyrillic** | Include a regular + bold TTF (or OTF) in `font-faces`. | These are simple glyphs; the engine will use the exact weight you list. | | **Arabic / Hebrew** | Add the appropriate Noto-Sans-Arabic / Noto-Sans-Hebrew files to `font-faces`. | Since GL JS 6.9.0 the RTL plugin is no longer needed; Native always uses HarfBuzz shaping when a local font is present. | | **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc.** | Provide the script-specific TTF and list its Unicode range. | From Native 6.15.0 onward these scripts are rendered as grapheme clusters by HarfBuzz; the glyph PBFs are ignored, so the local font is the only source. | | **CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean)** | **Option A (recommended):** ship a CJK font (e.g. `NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf`) and reference it in `font-faces`.
**Option B (smaller APK):** rely on the device’s built-in CJK system fonts by *omitting* the CJK entry from `font-faces`. The engine will fall back to the system font because the glyph request fails. | CJK glyph sets are huge. If you have enough storage you get consistent shapes by bundling your own font; otherwise you can let the OS pick the font (the result will vary by device). | | **Symbols that mix scripts** (e.g. “北京 Paris”) | Ensure **all** scripts used in the same label have a matching entry in `font-faces`. Description: implicit — Devanagari labels drawn letter by letter
prompt: Hindi labels on my MapLibre GL JS map come out wrong: vowel signs and conjuncts land in the wrong place, as if each letter were drawn on its own. My style has a glyphs URL that serves Noto Sans Devanagari. How do I fix it?

The upgrade path is far simpler. --- ## 2. Add a `font-faces` entry for Devanagari ### 2.1. No extra spaces, case-sensitive. | | `unicode-range` | Limits the file to Devanagari code points.
